name: Payne's Grey
lede: Payne's Grey is a dark, muted blue-grey that the English watercolorist William Payne mixed as a gentler stand-in for black, and two respected sources cannot agree on what he actually put in it.

sections.title: A teacher's substitute for black
sections.body: William Payne (1760-1830) was an English painter and etcher, a drawing-master who developed methods that considerably widened what watercolor could do, particularly in rendering sunlight and atmosphere [1]. Those methods, more than the specific grey he is remembered for today, are what made him briefly the most fashionable drawing-master in London [1]. Black was the traditional way to darken a wash, but Payne wanted something that organized shadows and values without the visually blunt result plain black gives a landscape, so he mixed his own dark, violet-leaning grey and recommended it to his students instead [1]. Wikipedia and Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary agree on when the name itself first appears in English print: 1835, five years after Payne's death [1][2]. That is a separate claim from our own graph's earliest-dated citation for this exact swatch, which comes from a different, later source, Ridgway's 1912 color-standards system [2] — the word is older than any of our own sources that measured this particular hex.

sections.title: Two formulas that disagree
sections.body:
What Payne actually mixed is not settled [1][3]. One account gives Prussian blue, yellow ochre and crimson lake [1]. A separate, respected source on indigo gives a different recipe entirely: lake, raw sienna and indigo [3]. Both are real, sourced claims, and this article does not pick a winner between them — what both agree on is the idea, a convenient, pre-mixed neutral tint built from pigments already on a watercolorist's palette, not a single mineral or dye of its own [1][3]. Balfour-Paul adds a practical reason indigo-based versions stayed popular into the twentieth century: the mix washes on more smoothly than a wash built straight from Prussian blue, and painters often reached for it specifically where Prussian blue would otherwise be the obvious choice [3]. Gurney offers a third formula again, black and ultramarine, and gives the real reason three sources can disagree: in his technical vocabulary, Payne's Grey is what painters call a convenience mixture, a blended paint sold under one recognizable name with no single pigment of its own, the same category a mixed paint-store "mauve" and phthalo yellow-green belong to [12]. A convenience mixture is defined by the result it reaches, not by one fixed recipe, so different manufacturers and painters filling the same gap were never guaranteed to use the same ingredients.

The name has its own small history of getting garbled in transmission. The Pigment Compendium notes that some older technical sources spell it "Pattison" or "Patterson" rather than Payne's, a slip that risks tangling the watercolorist's grey up with an unrelated nineteenth-century process for refining lead, named for a different man entirely, a metallurgist called Pattinson [11]. The two have nothing in common beyond a few accidentally shared letters.

sections.title: A wash for shadow, not a subject
sections.body: Payne's Grey is built to sit in the parts of a painting the eye is not meant to linger on [4][5]. One watercolorist working more than a century and a half after Payne describes the habit directly, illustrating a flying city for *Dinotopia: First Flight* (1999): to paint a minaret's shadowed lower half, he laid a Payne's gray wash first, under the rest of the color, specifically because shadow areas in watercolor cannot be premixed the way oil paint allows [4]. The glowing passageways beside it, lit after the sun had set in the scene, were painted afterward, over that same grey foundation [4]. That instinct shows up again and again in technical references: a working colorist's own pigment-matching charts list Payne's Gray repeatedly among the practical neutral blacks and greys, the colors chosen for structure and shade rather than for being looked at directly [5]. Garments in our own archive echo the same quiet, background role: a woven textile from Sardinia carries a near-match 2.8 units off, a nineteenth-century Chinese fragment 3.7 off, and a twentieth-century English fragment 4.0 off [6] — three continents, one unglamorous blue-grey.

sections.title: Its neighbors
sections.body: In the color graph, Payne's Grey sits 3.0 units from [[black-coral]], almost the same color [7]. [[delphinium]], 4.2 units off, is lighter; [[dark-orient-blue]], 4.3 off, is bluer; [[deep-slate-blue]], 4.7 off, is darker; [[blue-slate]], 5.0 off, is duller [7]. Its own named variant, [[deep-payne-s-grey]], sits 5.1 units away and is almost the same color again [7][2]. The family runs three named variants under the same root: [[dark-payne-s-grey]] is markedly darker still, [[deep-payne-s-grey]] is the one closest to the root color (the real look-alike edge above), and [[pale-payne-s-grey]] is lifted much higher in lightness, nearly a pastel version of the same hue — a sign of how useful one mixed neutral turned out to be, stretched across a whole tonal range under one family name [2]. Our own computed-nearest ISCC-NBS block for this hex and the real 1955 dictionary filing for the exact name Payne's Grey agree for once, both landing on block 186, "grayish blue," only 0.4 units apart [2]. On a painter's mixing wheel, its true complement sits nearest [[olive-brown]], [[pale-brown]] and [[mole-brown]] — three warm, dusty browns opposite a cold, muted blue-grey [7].

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Among design aesthetics, the closest full-palette matches near Payne's Grey are Tonalism, 2.9 units off on its neighbor Deep Slate-Blue, and Frutiger Aero, 3.7 off on Deep Payne's Grey, with Hypebeast a step further at 4.6 units on Black Coral [8]. Tonalism is the fitting one: an American painting movement built on muted, closely related tones is a natural late home for a pigment invented to soften contrast [8]. On screen, *Blade Runner 2049*'s cold, synthetic palette lands 4.2 units from this exact grey [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this grey in 380 of 23,778 paintings, about 1.6 percent as photographed; a stricter within-painting lens finds it in 143 [10]. That makes it more common than 63 percent of the named colors in the archive [10]. The single clearest number here is the role it plays once it is present: in 50 percent of its 143 clearest matches it sits as a hidden color, the least visible rank by lightness within the canvas, far ahead of any of the other four roles we measure [10]. That is exactly the part a painting draws least attention to, and exactly where Payne built his mixture to work [10].

It peaks century-wide in the 1900s, 1.9 percent of 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.8 times the expected rate, and the sharper single-decade peak is the 1910s, 2.5 percent of 523 paintings, 3.4 times expected [10]. It is also over-represented in paintings from India, 2.3 times expected across 721 paintings, and from France, 2.2 times expected across 3,443 [10]. The earliest match in the archive is from 1100, with 258 dated paintings carrying it through to 1950; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and an 1100 match sits more than seven centuries before any of our own sources date the name itself — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that anyone mixed this exact blend that early [10]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test.

questions.q: Why did William Payne mix his own grey instead of just using black?
choices: Plain black gave a visually blunt result in a landscape wash
Black pigment was too expensive in the 1790s
Black was banned from watercolor palettes
He was colorblind to true black
questions.answer: Plain black gave a visually blunt result in a landscape wash

questions.q: True or false: all our sources agree on the exact three pigments in the original Payne's Grey mixture.
What role does Payne's Grey most often play inside a painting, by our own archive's measurement?
choices: A hidden color, the least visible by lightness in the canvas
An even split across all roles
questions.answer: A hidden color, the least visible by lightness in the canvas

openers: Two respected sources disagree on what William Payne actually mixed into his own namesake grey.
Payne's Grey is built to hide: half the time our archive finds it, it is the least visible color on the whole canvas.

issues: Depth wave pilot: built from color-kb concordance (25 hits: Gurney, Balfour-Paul, Baty, Paterson, Pigment Compendium, St Clair) plus a web source for William Payne's biography, the color graph's real look-alikes and named variants, archive fieldnotes, and look/film/garment twins. States both disagreeing historical formulas rather than picking one.

Fresh-context fact-check (2026-10-09): found one unsupported qualitative claim (neighbors section said Deep Payne's Grey 'leans a touch greener', contradicting the real look-alike edge's own 'almost the same' tag); removed the invented nuance.
